decision.explanation: Dividing numerator and denominator by x² gives (100/x)/(1−1/x²), which tends to 0/1=0 as x→∞.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{100x}{{x}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[100x]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{100}{2x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The limit has form 0/0. Applying L'Hôpital's rule gives lim ln(x)/(2x−2), still 0/0. Applying it again gives lim (1/x)/2 = 1/2.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=1$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{[1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[{x}^{2}-2x+1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2x-2}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1-x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[2x-2]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0. Applying L'Hôpital's rule once gives ln(x+2)/(2x+2), again 0/0. Applying it a second time gives 1/[2(x+2)], which tends to 1/2 as x→−1.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=-1$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-x-1}{{x}^{2}+2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{[(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-x-1]}^{′}}{{[{x}^{2}+2x+1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}{2x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-x-1}{{x}^{2}+2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}{2x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)]}^{′}}{{[2x+2]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{(\frac{1}{x+2})}{2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{1}{2(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: As x→0+, the ratio has indeterminate form −∞/∞. L'Hôpital's rule gives cot(x)/(−csc²(x)) = −sin(x)cos(x), which tends to 0.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]}^{′}}{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{-{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡0\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Dividing by x² gives (5/x+1/x²)/(1+∛x/x²). As x→−∞, the numerator tends to 0 and the denominator tends to 1, so the limit is 0.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{5x+1}{{x}^{2}+\sqrt[3]{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{[5x+1]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}+\sqrt[3]{x}]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{5}{(2x+\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}})} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
